stem: What is the correct order of the strokes in a four-stroke engine?

options.content: Induction, compression, power, exhaust
Compression, induction, exhaust, power
Power, induction, compression, exhaust
Induction, power, compression, exhaust

stem: During the compression stroke of a petrol engine, which valves are open?

options.content: Neither valve
options.rationale: Correct: both are closed so the mixture can be compressed.

options.content: The inlet valve only
The exhaust valve only
Both valves

explanation: Both valves are closed during compression and power.

stem: Which stroke is the only one that does useful work on the piston?

options.content: Induction
options.rationale: The piston is moved by the crankshaft.

options.content: Compression
options.rationale: Work is done ON the gas.

options.content: Power
Exhaust

explanation: In the power stroke the burning gases push the piston down; the other strokes are driven by the flywheel.

stem: In a petrol engine, what part produces the spark that ignites the fuel-air mixture?
explanation: The spark plug ignites the compressed mixture at the start of the power stroke.

stem: What is the job of the carburettor?

options.content: To ignite the fuel
To mix petrol and air in the right proportions
To cool the engine
To turn up-and-down motion into rotation

explanation: The carburettor mixes fuel and air for efficient burning.

stem: A diesel engine needs a spark plug to ignite its fuel.
explanation: Diesel engines compress air so strongly that it becomes hot enough to ignite the injected diesel: compression ignition.

stem: Match each stroke with what happens.

right.content: Spark ignites the mixture; expanding gas pushes the piston down
Piston moves up; burnt gases pushed out through the exhaust valve
Piston moves down; fuel-air mixture drawn in through the inlet valve
Piston moves up; mixture squashed with both valves closed

explanation: The four strokes repeat in this order every two turns of the crankshaft.
hints: Two strokes have the piston moving down, two up.

stem: Why do car engines usually have four or more cylinders?

options.content: So that every stroke of each piston becomes a power stroke.
options.rationale: Each cylinder still has one power stroke in four.

options.content: Power strokes come more often, so it runs smoother and stronger.
So that each cylinder burns less fuel and runs cooler.
options.rationale: Not the main reason: smoothness and power are.

options.content: Because a single cylinder cannot hold a spark plug and valves.
options.rationale: A single cylinder can have both, as in small motorcycle engines.

explanation: With several cylinders firing at different times there is an even series of power strokes: smoother running and more power.
hints: How often does a single cylinder produce a power stroke?

stem: A car's air filter becomes blocked. What is the most likely result?

options.content: The engine runs cooler and its exhaust becomes cleaner
Fuel economy improves because less air is drawn in
options.rationale: Too little air wastes fuel: economy gets worse.

options.content: Incomplete combustion, producing black soot and carbon monoxide
The spark plug stops sparking at once and the engine cuts out completely
options.rationale: The spark plug is not affected directly.

explanation: Too little air for the fuel means incomplete burning: soot, carbon monoxide and wasted fuel.
hints: What does fuel need to burn completely?

stem: A transport company is choosing engines for its long-distance buses.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe two differences between the operation of a petrol engine and a diesel engine.

points.description: Petrol engine draws in a fuel-air mixture; diesel draws in air only (fuel is injected later)
Petrol ignites by a spark from a spark plug; diesel ignites by the heat of compression
Diesel compresses the air much more (higher compression)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest why diesel engines are chosen for the buses.

points.description: Diesel engines are more efficient, giving more kilometres per litre (better fuel economy)
They are strong and durable, suiting heavy vehicles and long distances

explanation: Diesel engines draw in air only, ignite by compression and are more economical and robust, which suits heavy buses.
hints: Think about ignition and what is drawn in.

stem: What does the choke do when a cold petrol engine is started?

options.content: Cools the engine while it warms up after starting
options.rationale: The choke does nothing to cool the engine.

options.content: Stops fuel reaching the cylinders until the engine is warm enough
Opens the exhaust valve to clear out burnt gases
options.rationale: That is the exhaust valve's job.

options.content: Cuts the air supply to give a richer, easier-to-light mixture

explanation: The choke restricts air so the mixture has more petrol, making a cold start easier.
